title: Given a sorted array of numbers and a target sum, find a pair of elements whose values add up exactly to the target and return their indices. Solve it with the two-pointer technique. (LeetCode: Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted)
shortTitle: Pair with Target Sum (Two Pointers on a Sorted Array)

s1_definition.profdef: The pair-with-target-sum problem asks you to locate two elements in a sorted array whose sum equals a given target. The optimal approach is the two-pointer technique: place one pointer at the start and one at the end, and move them toward each other based on whether the current sum is too small or too large. This runs in linear time and constant extra space because the array's sorted order lets each comparison eliminate one candidate permanently.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a list of pending settlement amounts already sorted from smallest to largest, and he needs to find exactly two settlements that together clear a target obligation of a fixed rupee amount. Instead of checking every possible pair, Priya stands at the smallest amount and Rajesh stands at the largest. If their two amounts add up to more than the target, Rajesh steps down to a smaller amount. If they add up to less, Priya steps up. They walk toward each other until the two amounts hit the target exactly.
s1_definition.oneliner: In a sorted array, start wide, then squeeze inward: too big means shrink the right, too small means grow the left.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The pair-with-target-sum problem asks you to locate two elements in a sorted array whose sum equals a given target. The optimal approach is the two-pointer technique: place one pointer at the start and one at the end, and move them toward each other based on whether the current sum is too small or too large. This runs in linear time and constant extra space because the array's sorted order lets each comparison eliminate one candidate permanently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a list of pending settlement amounts already sorted from smallest to largest, and he needs to find exactly two settlements that together clear a target obligation of a fixed rupee amount. Instead of checking every possible pair, Priya stands at the smallest amount and Rajesh stands at the largest. If their two amounts add up to more than the target, Rajesh steps down to a smaller amount. If they add up to less, Priya steps up. They walk toward each other until the two amounts hit the target exactly.

**One line to remember:** In a sorted array, start wide, then squeeze inward: too big means shrink the right, too small means grow the left.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach checks every pair, which is quadratic time. On a sorted array we can do much better. We keep a `left` index at position 0 and a `right` index at the last position. We compute `sum = arr[left] + arr[right]`. If the sum equals the target, we have found the pair. If the sum is greater than the target, the only way to reduce it is to decrease the larger value, so we move `right` one step left. If the sum is smaller than the target, the only way to increase it is to raise the smaller value, so we move `left` one step right.

This works because the array is sorted. When `arr[left] + arr[right]` is too large, `arr[left]` paired with anything to the right of the current `right` would be even larger, so `right` can never again be part of the answer with this `left`; we safely discard it. The same logic applies symmetrically. Each step eliminates exactly one element, so we touch each element at most once, giving linear time.

A small usage example in the finance domain: suppose settlement amounts are `[150, 300, 450, 700, 950]` and the target is `750`. We start with `left=0` (150) and `right=4` (950). The sum 1100 is too big, so `right` drops to 700. Now 150 plus 700 is 850, still too big, so `right` drops to 450. Now 150 plus 450 is 600, too small, so `left` rises to 300. Now 300 plus 450 is 750, which matches, and we return indices 1 and 2.

The senior-level nuance: the problem variant on LeetCode returns one-based indices, so we add one to each zero-based index before returning. Also, the two-pointer method assumes the input is already sorted; if it is not, sorting first costs `n log n`, and in that case a hash-map approach that remembers complements in a single linear pass is usually preferable because it does not require sorting.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the end-of-day settlement desk holds a list of outstanding transaction amounts that the clearing system already returns in sorted order. A regulator sometimes requires the desk to prove that a specific target obligation can be settled by combining exactly two outstanding transactions. Scanning every possible pair on a list of hundreds of thousands of transactions is painfully slow and would blow past the settlement window. This is exactly where the two-pointer technique helps: because the list is already sorted, we can find the matching pair in a single linear sweep.

Problem 2 — The desk also needs the result to be auditable, meaning it must report which two transactions were combined, not just that a combination exists. This is why we return the positions of the two amounts rather than a simple true or false.

The code will define a `SettlementPairFinder` class with a `findPair` method that takes the sorted amounts and a target, uses two pointers, and returns the pair of one-based positions. A small runnable demo seeds a sorted list of settlement amounts for Rajesh and prints the pair found for a target obligation. The demo uses `BigDecimal` for money correctness and a clean logger.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sorted amounts `[150, 300, 450, 700, 950]` and the target `750`.

Step 1: The finder places `left` at index 0 (amount 150) and `right` at index 4 (amount 950). Nothing has changed in the array; only the two pointers exist.

Step 2: The sum is 150 plus 950, which is 1100. That is greater than 750, so the method moves `right` down to index 3 (amount 700). The array is untouched.

Step 3: The sum is now 150 plus 700, which is 850. Still greater than 750, so `right` moves down to index 2 (amount 450).

Step 4: The sum is 150 plus 450, which is 600. That is less than 750, so the method moves `left` up to index 1 (amount 300).

Step 5: The sum is 300 plus 450, which is exactly 750. The method builds a `PairResult` with one-based positions 2 and 3 and their amounts, then returns it.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 5:45:00 PM com.bank.settlement.PairFinderDemo main
INFO: Target 750 settled by PairResult{pos 2 (300) + pos 3 (450)}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: sorted amounts [150, 300, 450, 700, 950], target = 750
    │
    ▼
  SettlementPairFinder.findPair()
    │ left=0 (150), right=4 (950)
    │
    ├─ sum=1100 > 750 ──→ right-- (now 700)
    │  sum= 850 > 750 ──→ right-- (now 450)
    │  sum= 600 < 750 ──→ left++  (now 300)
    │  sum= 750 = 750 ──→ MATCH
    ▼
  PairResult{pos 2 (300) + pos 3 (450), found=true}
    │
    ▼
  Output: INFO "Target 750 settled by ..."
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The pair-with-target-sum problem asks me to find two elements in a sorted array whose values add up to a given target, and the clean solution is the two-pointer technique that runs in linear time and constant space. I place one pointer at the start of the array and one at the end, compute the sum of the two values they point to, and then decide which pointer to move based on how that sum compares to the target.

The core insight that makes this correct is the sorted order of the array. When the current sum is larger than the target, the only way to make it smaller is to move the right pointer inward to a smaller value, and I can safely discard the old right element because pairing it with anything smaller on the left would only make the sum even larger. When the sum is too small, I move the left pointer inward to a larger value for the same reason in reverse. Each move permanently eliminates one element, so I touch each element at most once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this exact approach on the end-of-day settlement desk. The clearing system already returns outstanding transaction amounts in sorted order, and the regulator sometimes requires us to show that a specific target obligation can be cleared by combining exactly two outstanding transactions. A brute-force pair check over hundreds of thousands of transactions would miss the settlement window, so the two-pointer sweep gave us the answer in a single linear pass, and I returned the positions of the two transactions so the result was fully auditable.

The senior-level point I always add is about preconditions. The two-pointer method depends on the array being sorted. If the input were not sorted, I would either sort it first at an n-log-n cost or switch to a hash-map approach that remembers each element's required complement in a single pass, which avoids sorting entirely. Choosing between those depends on whether the data arrives sorted and whether I also need the original positions, and being explicit about that tradeoff is what separates someone who memorized a trick from someone who understands when to use it.
